course_description:
A great deal of resources and analysis are dedicated to war and violence, but comparatively little effort is directed to transforming the structural and cultural conditions that generate war or to addressing the injustices and traumas that arise from violence. The recently emerged sub-field of peacebuilding attempts to address these and related challenges by bringing together the theory and practice of conflict resolution, humanitarian assistance, and development. Among other goals, peacebuilding attempts to address the dynamics of entrenched civil conflict, structural injustice and other conflict causes to prevent the emergence of violent conflict and to address its effects. The challenges that accompany this work confront organisations from the United Nations to international non-government organisations and states from Afghanistan to Australia. In this course we develop an understanding of peacebuilding and critically engage with it at both a theoretical and practical level.

How to deal with the aftermath of violent ruptures and large-scale traumatic events presents a perennial challenge for social and political ordering. When the most visible and disruptive forms of violence end, the disruption, trauma and slow violence it has caused often does not. This course investigates some of the challenges caused by these ruptures and violent events by taking a broad understanding of what peacebuilding can entail, including conflict resolution, development, institution building, security sector reform, efforts to obtain justice, and the struggles of building peace in sites of ongoing settler colonialism. As a capstone course for the Peace and Conflict Studies major, the politics of peacebuilding will introduce the most recent debates within work on peacebuilding while giving students and opportunity to improve understanding of individual sites of enduring conflict around the world.ﾠ

course_aims: This course investigates peacebuilding as a fundamentally political endeavour, defined by contested visions for the future and understandings of conflict and conceptions of justice. The course begins with four weeks exploring conceptions of sociopolitical order for peacebuilding. After this, we investigate key components and issues in peacebuilding as mapped in the Learning Activities. We will tackle cutting edge topics including peacebuilding amidst populism and authoritarianism, relational peacebuilding beyond the human, space and place in peacebuilding, and coloniality and Indigenous peoples in peacebuilding. Learning in the course will take place through 13 seminars (including lectures, interactive discussion, and workshopping). You will engage with a peacebuilding case of your choice throughout the semester in completing your assessment items.

learning_outcomes.description: Appreciate the complex, contested and political nature of peacebuilding.
Understand the cultural foundations of dominant and innovative/ alternative approaches to political ordering for peacebuilding.

Demonstrate responsible use of generative AI to support peacebuilding research and analysis, while recognising the importance of human judgement and verification, contextual knowledge, and ethical considerations.

Collaborate effectively in teams to evaluate competing peacebuilding priorities, facilitate collective decisions, and communicate coherent and evidence-informed recommendations for preventing violent conflict and sustaining peace.
Explain key peacebuilding concepts and apply peacebuilding knowledge to ethical and social dilemmas in conflict-affected societies.

assessment_details.title: Peacebuilding Investment Board: Group Report (4000 words)
assessment_details.other_conditions: Work integrated learning, AI Required. See the conditions definitions
assessment_details.task_description: Each student will be assigned a group, who comprise the members of the Board of the Global Peacebuilding Fund (GPF), an international funding mechanism established to prevent the outbreak, escalation, continuation, and recurrence of violent conflict and support sustainable peace. GPF has US$1 billion available to invest over the next five years. Demand for funding significantly exceeds available resources, meaning difficult choices must be made about what to fund, where to invest, and which intiatives are most likely to contribute to sustainable peace. Your group’s task is to develop a 4000-word peacebuilding investment strategy report. The report should : 1 Begin with Executive Summary and brief overview of the strategic rationale guiding your funding decisions: Often when UN agencies, bilateral donors, and development banks decide where to channel funding they offer an overarching justification for why the activities are strategically aligned with the context, evidence, and intended outcomes. Your group is tasked with doing the same: to offer a strategic rationale for your funding decisions. A strategic rationale is an explanation and justification for why your group has chosen to invest in particular initiatives as the most appropriate and effective way to achieve the desired objective of sustainable peace. For example, should funding be prioritised based on: Greatest conflict risk(s)? On what basis is risk determined? Value for money: addressing ongoing conflicts or preventing future conflict? Political opportunity structure: political constraints/opportunities? Legitimacy or positionality of actor: UN-led efforts, state building/governance initiatives, or local/community peacebuilding? A particular region or conflict context? A particular type of initiative? governance, mediation and peace processes, climate adapatation, security, transitional justice, social cohesion, gender and youth, etc. Addressing the root causes of conflict? How are these assessed? Diversified funding portfolio or catalytic initiative (e.g., like the Rotary Polio Eradication Initiative) There is no single correct approach. However, your funding decisions should reflect a clear, coherent, and well-justified rationale for how your investment portfolio is going to advance sustainable peace. 2 Clearly identify what you are funding: Identify the institutions, initiatives, programs, or sectors receiving funding; the amount allocated to each; and any geographic or regional priorities in the funding allocation. Your peace investment portfolio should account for the full US$1billion. [Note: this may seem like a lot of money, but by comparison Australia’s ODA budget is ~$5.2bn for the 2026-27 financial year; before it was axed, USAID oversaw a budget of approximately $35bn/pa—so you have tough decisions to make!] 3 Justify your funding decisions: Explain and justify why these are good investments in peace based on: the best available evidence of what works (or does not work) in peacebuilding and conflict prevention; conflict data and analysis; cultural and ethical considerations; political feasibility; likelihood of impact; potential risks and limitations. 4 Identify how used AI: You are required to use generative AI tools for the purposes of synthesising the corpus of data, reports, and policy documents that you have acquired for your research. You are expected to select a significant and relevant body of information that would otherwise be unfeasible to analyse in a short period of time. You may use AI for other technical elements of the report (e.g. structuring), however you are required to include an annex to the report that provides an overview of how AI was used: What tasks did AI assist with? What AI platform did you use? What, if any, sources did you upload? Provide 3-5 examples of prompts that significantly influenced your analysis or funding decisions, and explain how they shaped your thinking. How did you verify AI-generated information? What were the limitations, biases, or weaknesses? Were there AI-generated recommendations that you rejected, why? You must strictly abide by copyright rules—meaning no copyrighted material should be uploaded into an AI platform. Groups will not be assessed on the extent to which they used AI or on their technological proficiency, but on their ability to use AI critically, transparently, and responsibly. Demonstrating awareness of AI’s limitations is just as important as demonstrating its utility. Read full task description Hide full task description

assessment_details.title: Critical Reflection (2500 words)
assessment_details.task_description: A critical reflection is a piece of writing which requires you to think about your experiences, challenges and successes, and create a plan of improvement for the future. Coherent thought and deliberate planning based on probable outcomes create the strongest critical reflections (as opposed to stream of consciousness and guesswork). Your task is to write a 2500-word critical reflection essay. It should: 1. Critically reflect on your funding strategy and process: Identify trade-offs you made : Because resources are limited, funding one initiative means not funding another. What trade-offs did your group face?; What initiatives or approaches did you choose not to fund, why? How did evidence drive your decision-making? What counted as reliable evidence? How did you work together as a group?: What was your most contested collective decision? How did you resolve it? What is one piece of advice you would give for more effective team work, based on your experience? 2. Drawing on specific examples from other group presentations, critically reflect on how your funding strategy and decisions compared to other groups. Consider questions such as: What different strategic rationales emerged across the class? Were some approaches more persuasive than others? What types of evidence were most effectively used? What evidence seemed the strongest versus most contested/uncertain? Did certain assumptions about peacebuilding appear to dominate decision-making? What were they? In retrospect, and based on what you learned from other group presentations, would you make different funding decisions? Why or why not? Reflect on the use of AI, both within your group and across the class. Your discussion should consider: whether AI performed well (or poorly) at particular tasks; any common errors, omissions, or biases that became apparent; examples where AI may have influenced funding decisions in problematic ways; whether/how policymakers should use AI in making complex peacebuilding decisions. 3. Draw on literature and debates we covered in the course to critically reflect on whether important issues were marginalised, overlooked, or undervalued in the funding exercise, or on whether specific efforts were made to meaningfully address these issues. Consider issues such as: culture; inclusion; local ownership; relational peace and Indigenous approaches; long-term versus short-term imperatives. 4. Reflecting on limitations in this funding exercise, propose one new directive/reform for the Global Peacebuilding Fund Board assignment that could improve future group’s decision-making processes, inclusivity, or effectiveness. Explain the problem your reform addresses and how it would improve future funding decisions. Please note: Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Translation (MT) are emerging tools that may support students in completing this assessment task. Students may appropriately use AI or MT in completing this assessment task. Students must clearly reference any use of AI or MT in each instance.
